title: National segmentation
text: The page documents the technical decisions made during the segmentation process.

title: National segmentation
text:
Rationale and objective
The South African Biodiversity Intactness Index (BII) requires a consistent spatial unit of assessment to which a broad land-use class, land-use intensity, and eventually species information can be linked. Here, that unit is an image-derived segment: a group of neighbouring 30 m pixels (10 m embeddings averaged to a fixed 30 m grid) with similar landscape characteristics.
A regular grid (also called a fishnet), that is typically used in broad scale spatial workflows, is straightforward to reproduce, but its boundaries are imposed without reference to the landscape. A grid cell can therefore split fields or plantations, or combine very different land uses, imposing artificial boundaries on the landscape. Segmentation can follow landscape variation more closely, potentially producing units that more closely align with underlying vegetation structure, land use patterns, and management units, which provides a more appropriate basis for assigning land use intensity and estimating biodiversity intactness. In GEE land-cover studies, SNIC-based objects gave more accurate and spatially coherent maps than per-pixel classification of the same imagery (Tassi and Vizzari 2020; Tassi et al. 2021).
Our aim in this part of the workflow is to select one nationally applicable segmentation configuration that balances land-cover homogeneity, recognisable landscape structure, consistency with the approximately 1 km analysis scale used in the regional BII, and a manageable number of units for national modelling. We tested various options for segmentation below.

title: National segmentation
text:
Data and segmentation methods

Inputs and projection
We used the 2022 Google Satellite Embedding V1 collection (Brown et al. (n.d.)). Each native 10 m pixel contained a 64-dimensional landscape representation. All 64 bands were supplied to Simple Non-Iterative Clustering (SNIC); i.e. they were not averaged across dimensions. SNIC formed connected objects from regularly spaced seeds according to feature similarity and spatial proximity (Achanta and Süsstrunk 2017).
The sensitivity tests used SANBI’s South African Albers Equal Area CRS (AEA_RSA_WGS84; WGS84 datum, central meridian 25° E, standard parallels 24° S and 33° S). The 10 m and 30 m grids shared a fixed origin and affine transforms of [10, 0, 0, 0, -10, 0] and [30, 0, 0, 0, -30, 0], respectively. A fixed projection prevented GEE display scale from determining SNIC resolution. The national run used the same CRS and 30 m grid.
An earlier national run used the native ~20 m grid of SANLC 2022 in WGS84 (EPSG:4326; asset SA_NLC_2022_GEO). It was superseded by the final 30 m Albers run described under National segmentation.
The 2022 South African National Land Cover (SANLC) classification was used to evaluate, not generate, segments. In the final national run it plays no part in segmentation: the study extent comes from the SANBI terrestrial boundary and no land-cover mask is applied, so land cover is linked to segments only after unique IDs have been assigned. Broad land-cover proportions were obtained from the BII crosswalk (NLC_reclass_BII_land_use_intensity), with protected-area overlap calculated separately. SANLC was assessed on the 10 m extraction grid during the sensitivity tests; its underlying land-cover information originated from the 20 m product.


Sensitivity analysis
Two contrasting mixed-use rectangles were drawn in GEE: CT (Cape Town, including urban, industrial, tree croplands and mountain landscapes) and EC (Eastern Cape, including settlements, agriculture, plantations and natural vegetation). Each was buffered by 5 km during segmentation. Segments intersecting the test-area boundaries were excluded from comparisons.
We compared SNIC seed spacings of 600, 800, 1,000 and 1,200 m using 10 m embeddings. We then compared 10 m and 30 m embedding inputs at approximately 1,000 m seed spacing. For the 30 m scenario, each embedding band was spatially averaged from 10 m, and size = 33 gave 990 m nominal spacing. Seed spacing controlled initial seed separation rather than final segment area.
compactness = 1, connectivity = 8 and a 5 km buffer were held constant. The tests used neighborhoodSize = 4 × size; the subsequent national run used 66 pixels (2 × 33, the GEE default) to reduce processing demands. This change was not separately sensitivity-tested.
For each segment, we calculated the proportions of settlements, timber plantations, tree crops, croplands and untransformed land. The assigned BII class followed the first qualifying >20% proportion in that order, followed by protected land (>20% protected-area overlap), otherwise untransformed land. Protected land was an overlapping designation rather than a mutually exclusive cover type.
We assessed segment count, median area, area-weighted homogeneity (largest broad land-cover share), the proportion of assessed area in segments ≥80% homogeneous, and allocation retention (mapped area of a class occurring within segments assigned to that class). Composition figures represented pooled mapped hectares within each assigned class, not the mean segment. Repeated IDs in the test CSVs were combined using area-weighted proportions and boundary segments excluded; this procedure did not verify national ID uniqueness, which is now done separately (see Globally unique segment IDs).

title: National segmentation
text:
Sensitivity results
Segmentation scenarios were evaluated using five metrics: (1) segment count, indicating computational requirements; (2) median segment area (ha); (3) mean homogeneity, calculated as the area-weighted mean proportion of the dominant land-cover class within each segment; (4) area ≥80% homogeneous, representing the percentage of total assessed area within segments dominated by a single land-cover class (≥80%); and (5) transformed land-cover retention, representing the proportion of mapped settlements, croplands, tree croplands and plantations occurring within segments assigned to their corresponding BII land-use class. Additionally, pooled land-cover composition was calculated to assess the mixture of land covers within each assigned BII class. Together, these metrics assessed the trade-off between computational efficiency and land-use representation.

1. Seed spacing
Increasing seed spacing reduced segment counts but increased land-cover mixing (Table 1). Moving from 800 to 1,000 m reduced segments by 36.9% in CT and 37.0% in EC, with homogeneity declining by only 1.1 and 2.1%, respectively. Median areas at 1,000 m were 91.0 ha (CT) and 89.8 ha (EC), close to the regional BII’s 100 ha grid scale. We therefore selected approximately 1,000 m seed spacing.

title: National segmentation
National segmentation
text:
Globally unique segment IDs
Because GEE processes images in tiles, SNIC is computed tile by tile across the country. Although SNIC considers neighbouring pixels when delineating segments (neighborhoodSize), the resulting raw IDs are not globally unique: spatially disconnected segments can share the same ID. Globally unique IDs are essential for consistently linking land use, land-use intensity, species data and other attributes to individual segments. Ensuring this uniqueness requires an additional processing step, complicated by the size of the national raster (2.54 billion cells) and by the integer data types that different GIS platforms support. This section documents how every segment received a unique Int32 ID, why the GEE and R options were not suitable, and how the result was verified, in enough detail to reproduce it.






Summary




Result: 1,268,426 segments with IDs 1 to 1,268,426 in a single Int32 GeoTIFF on the original 30 m grid, plus a lookup table linking each ID to its raw SNIC ID and pixel count.
Why relabel: 14,110 raw SNIC IDs occur as two or more spatially separate segments (29,735 segments). Most are single SNIC clusters cut into pieces by GEE’s 256 × 256-pixel processing tiles; 207 are unrelated clusters that share the same ID by chance.
Why not GEE or terra: ee.Image.connectedComponents() returns Int64 and masks objects larger than 1,024 pixels. The installed terra::patches() (terra 1.8-29) runs only in memory (75.6 GB needed here), indexes cells with 32-bit integers and is known to crash R; it stops with “cannot do this for large rasters”.
Method: out-of-core connected-component labelling in strips, with union-find to join segments across strip boundaries (Python: cc3d, SciPy, rasterio), called from R. About 4 minutes on a 32 GB laptop; peak memory 3.8 GB.
Verification: an independent relabelling (scikit-image, different strip boundaries) produced the identical 1,268,426 segments one-to-one; all 2.73 billion pairs of adjacent pixels obey the segment rule; a full re-run reproduced every pixel value exactly.




Why the raw SNIC IDs are not unique
A segment is defined here as a 4-connected region of identical raw SNIC ID: a set of pixels with the same raw ID, each linked to the next through a shared pixel edge (not just a corner). This matches connectivity = 4 in SNIC, where clusters grow only through edge neighbours (Achanta and Süsstrunk 2017), and it is the same rule used by terra::patches(values = TRUE, directions = 4) and WhiteboxTools Clump (diag = FALSE). NoData pixels never belong to a segment; a raw ID of 0 is treated as a valid ID.
The raw IDs span almost the whole Int32 range (−2,147,477,888 to 2,147,481,461) and behave like random 32-bit numbers rather than a 1, 2, 3 … sequence. They are not unique: the raster contains 1,252,801 distinct raw IDs but 1,268,426 separate segments. 14,110 raw IDs occur as two or more spatially separate segments (29,735 segments in total; at most 6 per raw ID). Joining species or land-use data on the raw ID would therefore pool data from different places.
Two mechanisms explain the repeats. They can be told apart by the distance between the pieces that share a raw ID (Table 7).
Table 7. Raw SNIC IDs that occur as more than one segment, grouped by the largest distance between the centroids of their pieces.

Clusters cut by GEE tiles (13,901 raw IDs). GEE computes SNIC tile by tile and stitches the tiles together. The neighborhoodSize parameter (66 pixels here) reduces, but does not remove, tile-boundary artefacts. Where neighbouring tiles disagree slightly about a cluster’s extent, the cluster keeps its raw ID but can end up as several disconnected pieces. Two observations support this:

The 9,063 segments smaller than 10 pixels sit on a regular grid with a 256-pixel spacing. 95.0% of them lie within 2 pixels of a row or column of that grid, compared with 3.9% expected at random and 4.7% for all segments. This matches GEE’s 256 × 256-pixel computation tiles.
72.5% of the smaller pieces of cut clusters (n = 15,411) also lie on these tile edges (Figure 3).

Chance collisions (207 raw IDs). If 1,252,801 IDs are drawn at random from the 232 possible 32-bit values, the expected number of pairs sharing an ID is
\[
E \approx \frac{n^2}{2 \times 2^{32}} = \frac{1{,}252{,}801^2}{8{,}589{,}934{,}592} \approx 183,
\]
which is the same order as the 207 raw IDs whose pieces lie 50 km or more apart.






Figure 3: Example of one SNIC cluster (raw ID 1,888,322,453; red outline, left) that GEE cut into three separate pieces along a 256-pixel processing-tile edge (dashed lines). After relabelling (right), each piece is its own segment with its own ID. Background colours are random per ID; 4.2 × 4.2 km window.



Both problems are solved by relabelling: every 4-connected region of identical raw ID receives its own ID, so the pieces of a cut cluster become separate segments. The 9,063 fragments under 10 pixels make up 0.71% of segments and 0.002% of the mapped area (2,628 ha).


Options considered
GEE connectedComponents(). ee.Image.connectedComponents() can identify image objects and assign a unique ID to each: all pixels belonging to an object receive the same integer, in an additional labels band based on the connectivity of pixels in the first band of the image. However, the output is a 64-bit integer (Int64) raster, whereas SNIC outputs signed 32-bit integer (Int32) cluster IDs. Many GIS applications and raster-processing tools have limited support for Int64 values, whereas Int32 is widely compatible and provides more than enough unique IDs for our segments. In addition, connectedComponents() limits objects to maxSize = 1,024 connected pixels and masks larger ones. At 30 m, 1,024 pixels are only 92 ha, and 54.8% of the national segments (69.8% of the labelled area) are larger. The function was therefore considered inappropriate; the raw SNIC labels are exported as Int32 and unique IDs are assigned outside GEE.
terra::patches() in R. The original plan was terra::patches(snic, values = TRUE, directions = 4, ...). With the installed terra version (1.8-29) this cannot work for a national 30 m raster. We checked the package’s C++ source (src/patches.cpp, which implements patches(values = TRUE) as the method patches2) and terra’s own memory estimate (terra::mem_info()), summarised in Table 8.
Table 8. Limitations of terra::patches(values = TRUE) in terra 1.8-29 (Hijmans 2025) for this raster.



Limitation in terra 1.8-29
Consequence for the 2,538,138,372-cell raster




In-memory only: the function first checks whether the raster fits in memory and otherwise stops with “cannot do this for large rasters” (the block-by-block version is commented out in the source)
mem_info() reports 75.6 GB needed versus 8.9 GB allowed (70% of the free RAM on a 32 GB laptop), so it stops immediately


Reads all cell values into one vector of 8-byte doubles and allocates a second one for the patch numbers
2 × 2.54 billion × 8 bytes = 40.6 GB, more than the laptop’s total RAM


Cell positions are passed as 32-bit integers (const int &i)
The largest 32-bit integer is 2,147,483,647, so cell indices overflow from row 39,853 of 47,102 onwards (the southern ~15% of the raster), giving out-of-bounds memory access


Recursive depth-first search: one nested function call per pixel of a patch
The maintainer described it as “not memory safe yet”; issue #1758, “patches(, values=TRUE) crashes R”, was reported for an 8-million-cell raster on a 64 GB machine



patches() was rewritten for terra 1.9-1 (pull request #2006, January 2026). The new version replaces the depth-first search with a block-wise, two-pass union-find, which is the same strategy used below. That version has not been tested on this raster; it may allow an R-only workflow in future.
WhiteboxTools Clump. On a 973 × 960-pixel test raster it produced exactly the same segments as terra::patches() and the method below (909 segments; see Verification). It was not tested at national scale because it requires too much RAM.


Method: out-of-core connected-component labelling
Assigning IDs to connected regions is a standard image-processing task called connected-component labelling. A raster too large to hold in memory can be processed in horizontal strips with the classic two-pass approach (Wu, Otoo, and Suzuki 2009):

label each strip on its own;
record where a region continues across the boundary (seam) between two strips;
merge those records with a union-find (disjoint-set) algorithm (Tarjan 1975), so each region gets exactly one ID.

Only one strip is in memory at a time, so memory use does not depend on the size of the raster (Figure 4).






flowchart TD
    A["Raw SNIC raster<br/>Int32, 2.54 billion cells"] --> B["Read one strip<br/>2,048 rows x 53,886 columns"]
    B --> C["Label 4-connected regions of<br/>identical raw ID in the strip (cc3d)"]
    C --> D["Make labels unique across strips<br/>(add offset) and record seam links"]
    D -->|"next strip"| B
    D --> E["Union-find: merge linked labels;<br/>number segments 1..N in raster order"]
    E --> F["Pass 2: relabel every strip and write<br/>Int32 GeoTIFF + lookup table"]
    F --> G["Independent verification<br/>(scikit-image, different strips)"]
    G -->|"all checks pass"| H["Final raster, lookup CSV, QC report"]




Figure 4: Workflow of 01b_assign_unique_segment_ids.py. The raw raster is read in strips twice (pass 1 and pass 2) and twice more for the independent verification.





The steps below follow the section numbers in the annotated script 01b_assign_unique_segment_ids.py.
1. NoData encoding (script section 2). Connected-component libraries treat 0 as background, but 0 could be a valid SNIC ID. Each Int32 value is therefore re-interpreted as an unsigned 32-bit integer with its sign bit flipped. This one-to-one mapping sends only the NoData value to 0 and needs no extra memory (Table 9).

2. Strip labelling (pass 1, script section 3). The raster is read in 23 strips of 2,048 rows across the full width (110 million cells, 0.44 GB per strip). In each strip, the C++ library cc3d (Silversmith 2026) labels every 4-connected region of identical key with a local number 1…n. Adding the number of labels already issued in earlier strips (an offset) makes these provisional labels unique across the whole raster. Pass 1 produced 1,303,109 provisional labels in about 15 s.
3. Seam links (pass 1). Under 4-connectivity, pixels in two different strips can only touch vertically. A region can therefore cross a seam only where the last row of one strip and the first row of the next have the same raw ID in the same column. Each such pair of provisional labels is recorded once (Table 10). Diagonal contacts are ignored. Pass 1 recorded 34,683 seam links.

4. Union-find and numbering (script section 4). Provisional labels become the nodes of a graph and seam links its edges. The connected components of this graph are the segments. This also handles regions that cross several seams, or whose arms only meet further down (for example a U shape), because the merge is transitive. SciPy’s connected_components() (Virtanen et al. 2020) performs the union-find step. Segments are numbered 1 to N in the order in which their first pixel is met when reading the raster row by row from the top-left corner. The numbering is therefore consecutive, has no gaps and is identical every time the same input is processed. The 1,303,109 provisional labels resolve to 1,268,426 segments, far below the Int32 maximum of 2,147,483,647.
5. Relabelling and writing (pass 2, script section 5). Storing the provisional labels between passes would need a 10 GB temporary file. Instead, each strip is read and labelled again. Labelling is deterministic, and the label count and a CRC-32 checksum are compared with pass 1 to prove it. A small lookup array then converts each local label to its final ID, and the strip is written to the output GeoTIFF (Table 11). At the same time, the pixel count and raw SNIC ID of every segment are collected. If any final ID were found with two different raw IDs, the run would stop; this count was 0.

6. Lookup table and QC report (script section 7). A CSV with one row per segment (segment_id, raw_snic_id, n_pixels) and a plain-text QC report are written. The raster is first written under a temporary name (*.partial.tif) and only renamed after it has passed verification, so a failed run never leaves a final-looking file.
Efficiency. On a Windows laptop with 32 GB RAM and 24 logical cores, pass 1 took about 15 s, pass 2 with writing about 45 s, verification 2–2.5 minutes and overviews 15–20 s: 3.5–4 minutes in total across two runs. Peak memory was 3.8 GB, compared with at least 40 GB for any approach that holds the whole raster in memory. The 563 MB compressed input is read four times (twice for labelling, twice for verification) using all CPU cores for decompression (rasterio/GDAL), and no large temporary files are written. NumPy (Harris et al. 2020) handles all array operations.


Verification
The script verifies the file it has written against an independent relabelling. This uses a different library (scikit-image, Walt et al. (2014), instead of cc3d) and a different strip height (1,000 instead of 2,048 rows), so none of its seams coincide with those used to create the IDs. Every pixel is compared (Table 12). The output only receives its final file name if every check passes.

Additional checks:

Comparison with terra and WhiteboxTools. On the 973 × 960-pixel QA raster (data/benchmark_clumps), the method produced the same 909 segments as terra::patches(values = TRUE, directions = 4) and WhiteboxTools Clump, one-to-one. That raster has only 860 distinct raw IDs, so 49 additional segments are pieces of repeated raw IDs.
Algorithm tests. Before the national run, strip-wise results were compared with labelling the whole array in memory, for strip heights down to a single row. The cases were synthetic patterns designed to break seam handling (combs joined only at the top or bottom, a serpentine region crossing every seam, checkerboards that repeat the same values, a raw ID of 0, extreme Int32 values, all-NoData strips) and a real 6,000 × 7,000-pixel window of the national raster (39,572 segments). All were identical.
Check in R. 01_segment_ids.R (step 4) reopens the result with terra and confirms the data type (INT4S), the grid, IDs 1 to N, and agreement of the NoData pattern and raw IDs with the raw raster at 20,000 random cells.
Reproducibility. Running 01_segment_ids.R again end to end produced a lookup table that was byte-for-byte identical and the same value in all 2,538,138,372 raster cells (logs/segment_id_qc_reproduction_run.txt).

Using the IDs in the next step, for example to attach species occurrence points to segments in R:
library(terra)
seg <- rast("output/BII_segments_SA_uniqueID_AEA_30m_2022.tif")
lut <- data.table::fread("output/BII_segments_SA_uniqueID_AEA_30m_2022_lookup.csv")

pts <- vect(occ, geom = c("lon", "lat"), crs = "EPSG:4326")   # occ: data.frame of records
pts <- project(pts, crs(seg))                                 # to SA Albers
occ$segment_id <- extract(seg, pts)$segment_id                # NA outside the labelled area
occ <- merge(occ, lut, by = "segment_id", all.x = TRUE)       # add raw ID and segment size


Raster to vector
Polygonisation is not needed to assign unique IDs or to calculate land-use allocation and intensity: these zonal statistics can be computed directly on the raster. If vector geometries are needed later (e.g. to associate species distributions with segments), we will vectorise with open-source software for reproducibility: GDAL Polygonize, accessed through QGIS or in R with the gdalraster package.
Self-intersecting polygons need to be considered when vectorising. E.g. a square pixel may share a corner with its segment, but 3 borders with the neighbouring segment. When this pixel converts to a polygon, the connectedness (connectivity) parameter determines whether it remains with its original segment’s polygon (i.e. a multipart polygon) or becomes its own polygon. gdalraster explicitly warns that 8-connected can produce invalid geometries (which ArcPro for e.g. can’t read). Because the segments were built and labelled with 4-connectivity, vectorising with 4-connectedness keeps polygons consistent with the segment IDs: every ID is exactly one 4-connected region, so it becomes exactly one polygon (possibly with holes).


How to reproduce
Software. Windows 11, R 4.3.3 with terra 1.8-29 and rgeedim 0.4.0, and Python 3.13.0. The Python packages are pinned in requirements.txt: numpy 2.5.5, scipy 1.18.1, connected-components-3d 4.1.1, scikit-image 0.26.0 and rasterio 1.5.2, which includes GDAL 3.12.2. They are installed into a project-local virtual environment (.venv).
Scripts (in the Segment_ids project; each script is annotated section by section):

01_segment_ids.R: the workflow in R. Step 0 creates .venv and installs requirements.txt if it is missing (internet is needed once). Step 1 downloads the GEE asset only if the raw raster is not on disk. Step 2 checks the raw raster. Step 3 calls the Python script. Step 4 runs the R spot checks.
01b_assign_unique_segment_ids.py: assigns and verifies the unique IDs (sections 0–7 as described above).
01c_raw_id_diagnostics.py (optional): the diagnostics in Table 7.

Run. Set root at the top of 01_segment_ids.R to the local project folder and run the script. The script stops rather than overwrite existing output, so delete or rename earlier outputs first. Equivalent commands without R, from the project folder:
py -3.13 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv\Scripts\python.exe 01b_assign_unique_segment_ids.py

Core of the algorithm (Python excerpt)





INT32_MIN = -2147483648

def to_key(raw):                       # NoData (INT32_MIN) -> 0; every other value -> unique non-zero
    key = raw.view(np.uint32)
    key ^= np.uint32(0x80000000)
    return key

# ---- pass 1: label each strip, offset its labels, record seam links ----
offsets, links, total, prev_key = [], [], 0, None
for r0 in range(0, height, 2048):
    key = to_key(read_strip(r0))
    lab, n = cc3d.connected_components(key, connectivity=4, return_N=True, out_dtype=np.uint32)
    if prev_key is not None:           # same column, both valid, identical raw ID across the seam
        m = (key[0] == prev_key) & (key[0] != 0)
        pairs = np.column_stack((prev_lab[m].astype(np.int64) + prev_off,
                                 lab[0][m].astype(np.int64) + total))
        links.append(np.unique(pairs, axis=0))
    offsets.append(total)
    prev_key, prev_lab, prev_off = key[-1].copy(), lab[-1].copy(), total
    total += n

# ---- union-find over provisional labels (node 0 = background) ----
links = np.concatenate(links)
g = coo_matrix((np.ones(len(links)), (links[:, 0], links[:, 1])), shape=(total + 1, total + 1))
ncomp, comp = connected_components(g, directed=False)
# final[p] = segment ID of provisional label p: components ranked by their smallest label -> 1..N

# ---- pass 2: relabel each strip with a small lookup array and write it ----
for i, r0 in enumerate(range(0, height, 2048)):
    key = to_key(read_strip(r0))
    lab, n = cc3d.connected_components(key, connectivity=4, return_N=True, out_dtype=np.uint32)
    lut = np.empty(n + 1, np.int32)
    lut[0] = INT32_MIN                                   # background -> NoData
    lut[1:] = final[offsets[i] + 1: offsets[i] + n + 1]  # local label -> final ID
    dst.write(lut[lab], 1, window=Window(0, r0, width, lab.shape[0]))
Simplified excerpt; see 01b_assign_unique_segment_ids.py for the complete, annotated code including the determinism checks and verification.









Code for Figure 3 (R)





library(terra)
raw <- rast("data/raw/SA_SNIC_2022_30m_download.tif")
ids <- rast("output/BII_segments_SA_uniqueID_AEA_30m_2022.tif")
lut <- data.table::fread("output/BII_segments_SA_uniqueID_AEA_30m_2022_lookup.csv")
dup_raw <- 1888322453; x0 <- 341296; y0 <- -3460398; half <- 2100
e  <- ext(x0 - half, x0 + half, y0 - half, y0 + half)
rw <- crop(raw, e, snap = "out"); iw <- crop(ids, e, snap = "out")
recode <- function(r) { v <- values(r)[, 1]; u <- unique(v[!is.na(v)])
                        list(r = setValues(r, match(v, u)), n = length(u)) }
rr <- recode(rw); ir <- recode(iw)
pr <- as.polygons(rw, dissolve = TRUE); pu <- as.polygons(iw, dissolve = TRUE)
pieces <- lut$segment_id[lut$raw_snic_id == dup_raw]
# 256-pixel GEE tile edges: row phase 13, column phase 4 (01c_raw_id_diagnostics.py)
xe <- xmin(raw) + seq(4, ncol(raw), by = 256) * 30
ye <- ymax(raw) - seq(13, nrow(raw), by = 256) * 30
pal <- function(n, s) { set.seed(s); sample(hcl.colors(n, "Pastel 1")) }
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(rr$r, col = pal(rr$n, 3), legend = FALSE, axes = FALSE, main = "Raw SNIC IDs from GEE")
lines(pr, col = "grey25", lwd = 0.5); abline(v = xe, h = ye, lty = 2)
lines(pr[pr$raw_snic_id == dup_raw, ], col = "red", lwd = 3)
plot(ir$r, col = pal(ir$n, 4), legend = FALSE, axes = FALSE, main = "Globally unique segment IDs")
lines(pu, col = "grey25", lwd = 0.5); abline(v = xe, h = ye, lty = 2)

text(pp, labels = format(pp$segment_id, big.mark = ","), inside = TRUE, halo = TRUE, font = 2)





Notes and open decisions

Small tile-edge fragments. The 9,063 segments under 10 pixels (0.002% of the area) are genuine separate regions under the 4-connectivity rule, mostly slivers along GEE tile edges. Decide whether to keep them, merge them into the neighbouring segment they share the longest edge with, or exclude them before linking species data.
IDs belong to this segmentation. The unique IDs are deterministic for this raw raster (a re-run reproduced them exactly), but any change to the SNIC inputs, parameters, extent or grid changes the segments and therefore the IDs. Keep the raster and lookup table together, and version them with any product derived from them.
Overviews are for display only; terra::extract(), zonal statistics and other analyses read the full-resolution data.

Exploratory comparison with a regular grid
In an earlier northern Limpopo case study, image-derived segments were compared with regular 1 × 1 km cells using broad land-cover proportions and the same BII assignment rules. Segments more often contained a higher proportion of their assigned cover, and their assigned class more often matched the dominant cover, particularly for transformed land uses. This was an exploratory comparison, separate from the CT/EC parameter selection, and did not measure classification accuracy. title: South African BII land use intensity workflow
text:
Workflow summary
This workflow combines the South African National Land Cover (NLC) 2022, the South African National Protected Area Database (SAPAD) and biome-specific ecocsystem condition data to produce segment-based land use and land use intensity layers to develop a South African Biodiversity Intactness Index.
The unit of assessment is a spatial segment rather than an individual raster pixel. At the end of the workflow, each segment receives:

one dominant BII land use class; and
one land use intensity estimate between 0 and 1.

The pages are split into four sections:

National segmentation
National land use reclassification
National segment land use and intensity allocation
Context-specific land use intensity score refinement of “untransformed”

title: Land use intensity
text:
Summary
We used the South African National Land Cover (SANLC) dataset to assign both the broad land use to each segment and estimate land use intensity because it provides a nationally consistent and high-resolution representation of land cover that was not available across sub-Saharan Africa for the original BII assessment. SANLC is already used by SANBI in the National Biodiversity Assessment and other national biodiversity monitoring applications, providing consistency with established South African biodiversity products. Its regular update cycle (approximately every four years) also means that the BII land use and intensity layers can be updated using the same underlying national dataset, supporting repeatable monitoring of changes through time.

title: Land use intensity
section: Linking intensity to the expert assessments
text:
Linking intensity to the expert assessments
The BII experts estimated the abundance remaining for each species group under specified landscape scenarios, relative to an intact reference. For settlements, croplands and tree croplands, paired scenarios define the low- and high-intensity endpoints of an intensity gradient. Timber plantations were represented by a single intensive scenario.
For the sub-Saharan African BII, separate spatial proxies were used to estimate intensity within each broad land use. Relevant variables were standardised to 0–1, combined with equal weights, and rescaled within each broad land use class. For example, settlement intensity used settlement extent and population density, while cropland intensity used crop cover, field size and nitrogen inputs.
The South African implementation differs slightly because the 73-class SANLC product provides substantially more detailed information on the composition of each landscape. We use those subclasses to represent the within-class intensity of the land use assigned to a segment, while also explicitly accounting for the proportion of the segment converted to any non-natural land use.

SANLC intensity crosswalk
For transparency, the SANLC subclasses used to characterise within-class land use intensity were assigned to low, medium and high intensity categories and converted to scores of 0, 0.5 and 1, respectively. Timber plantations were treated as a single high-intensity class with a fixed score of 1.

These scores represent relative intensity within each broad land use class, rather than a common ecological impact scale across all classes. The final segment-level intensity for non-natural classes is therefore obtained by averaging the assigned-class mean intensity with the total proportion of the terrestrial segment occupied by all non-natural land uses.


Segment intensity calculation
We calculated intensity for each segment by using the average of the proportion of non-natural land cover and mean intensity score of the assigned braod land use.
For each segment, the first component is the area-weighted mean intensity of SANLC pixels belonging to the broad land use assigned to that segment:
\[
\bar{I}_{c,s}
=
\frac{\sum_i a_i I_i}
     {\sum_i a_i}
\]
where:

\(\bar{I}_{c,s}\) is the mean subclass intensity for assigned class \(c\) in segment \(s\);
\(I_i\) is the intensity score of pixel \(i\);
\(a_i\) is its area; and
only valid pixels belonging to the assigned broad land use are included.

The second component is the proportion of the terrestrial segment covered by all non-natural BII land uses combined:
\[
P_{\mathrm{non-natural},s}
=
P_{\mathrm{settlement},s}
+
P_{\mathrm{timber},s}
+
P_{\mathrm{treecrop},s}
+
P_{\mathrm{cropland},s}
\]
The final segment intensity for settlements, tree croplands and croplands is:
\[
I_s =
\frac{
\bar{I}_{c,s}
+
P_{\mathrm{non-natural},s}
}{2}
\]
This gives equal weight to:

how intensive the assigned land use is, based on its detailed SANLC subclasses; and
how much of the rest of the segment has been converted away from natural land.

For example, if a settlement-assigned segment has a mean settlement intensity of 0.8 and 90% of its terrestrial area is covered by settlements, croplands, tree croplands or timber plantations, its final intensity is:
\[
I_s = \frac{0.8 + 0.9}{2} = 0.85
\]
This allows two segments assigned to the same broad land use to differ not only because their mapped subclasses differ, but also because one occurs in a more extensively transformed landscape.


Timber plantations
Timber plantations are treated separately because the BII expert elicitation used a single plantation scenario rather than a low-to-high plantation gradient. Their assigned-class intensity is therefore fixed at 1.
The segment-level intensity is still adjusted for the total amount of non-natural land:
\[
I_s =
\frac{
1
+
P_{\mathrm{non-natural},s}
}{2}
\]
Thus, a timber-assigned segment that is 80% non-natural receives an intensity of 0.9.


Protected lands
Protected lands are currently assigned an intensity of 0. Protected status is treated as a management designation rather than part of the non-natural proportion.
This value represents the low-pressure protected scenario used in the BII land use framework and should not be interpreted as a direct measurement of protected-area effectiveness or ecological condition.


Untransformed lands
In progress
Intensity for segments assigned to Untransformed lands will be calculated separately. The land use intensity of land that has not been converted cannot be inferred reliably from SANLC natural cover subclasses alone because natural vegetation may still experience substantial grazing, browsing, harvesting or other land use pressures.
The sub-Saharan BII estimated intensity in untransformed lands primarily from livestock density and nitrogen inputs, with livestock pressure standardised within rainfall and soil nutrient contexts. For the South African implementation, additional pressure and condition datasets can be used where they improve on these broad proxies.
Potential inputs include livestock pressure relative to carrying capacity and mapped degradation or condition products being developed at SANBI. For example, in the Thicket biome, remotely sensed estimates of grazing intensity could help distinguish rangeland use intensity within segments otherwise classified as untransformed.
This component will be developed separately so that transformation intensity in the four non-natural classes is not conflated with ecological pressure or degradation in remaining natural vegetation.

title: Land use intensity
text:
Class-specific implementation

Settlements
Endpoints: mixed settlements → dense urban.

The South African approach uses SANLC settlement subclasses to distinguish within-class intensity. Vegetated formal and informal residential areas and villages are assigned intermediate scores, highly transformed residential, commercial, industrial, transport and mining classes are assigned high scores, and urban recreational classes are assigned low scores.
The mean settlement score is then averaged with the total non-natural proportion of the segment.


Croplands
Endpoints: non-intensive smallholder croplands → intensive large-scale croplands.


Commercial annual crops, sugarcane and other intensive commercial crop classes are assigned high intensity. Subsistence/small-scale annual crops and SANLC smallholding classes are assigned to the Croplands broad class at low intensity, reflecting the non-intensive smallholder endpoint more closely.
The mean cropland score is then averaged with the total non-natural proportion of the segment.


Tree croplands
Endpoints: non-intensive smallholder croplands → tree-crop plantations.

Commercial orchards and vines are currently assigned high intensity. Their mean assigned-class intensity is averaged with the total non-natural proportion of the segment.


Timber plantations
Single scenario: timber plantations.

All plantation subclasses are treated as the single intensive plantation scenario. Their assigned-class intensity is fixed at 1 and averaged with the total non-natural proportion.

title: Land use intensity
section: Difference from the sub-Saharan BII approach
text:
Difference from the sub-Saharan BII approach
The two approaches share the same conceptual aim: representing the intensity of human land use at a landscape scale so that mapped land uses correspond as closely as possible to the scenarios assessed by experts.
The main difference is how intensity is “spatialised”.
The sub-Saharan BII relied on separate pressure proxies such as population density, mapped land use extent, field size, nitrogen inputs and livestock density. These variables were standardised and combined to produce a relative intensity score within each broad class.
The South African BII makes greater use of the detailed SANLC classification. The intensity of the assigned class is first estimated from its mapped subclasses and then combined with the total proportion of the segment occupied by non-natural land uses. This explicitly incorporates landscape transformation into the segment score and reduces the dependence on separate continental-scale intensity proxies where detailed national land-cover information is available.
The approach remains consistent with the landscape-scale interpretation of the expert elicitation: intensity is intended to characterise the overall human modification represented by a segment, rather than the condition of an isolated land-cover pixel.

title: Broad land use allocation
text:
We used the South African National Land Cover (SANLC) dataset to assign broad land use and estimate land use intensity because it provides a nationally consistent and high-resolution representation of land cover that was not available across sub-Saharan Africa for the original BII assessment. SANLC is already used by SANBI in the National Biodiversity Assessment and other national biodiversity monitoring applications, providing consistency with established South African biodiversity products. Its regular update cycle (approximately every four years) also means that the BII land use and intensity layers can be updated using the same underlying national dataset, supporting repeatable monitoring of changes through time.
The aim of this section of the workflow is to assign each segment one dominant BII land use class following an expert decision tree.

title: Broad land use allocation
Broad land use allocation
section: 2. Assign one BII land use class
text:
2. Assign one BII land use class
A candidate class becomes eligible for assignment when it covers more than 20% of the segment.
The classes are evaluated in the following priority order:

Settlements
Timber plantations
Tree croplands
Croplands
Protected lands
Untransformed lands

Where multiple classes exceed 20%, the class with the highest priority is assigned. Therefore the decision tree logic is:
IF settlement proportion > 0.20 assign Settlement
ELSE IF timber proportion > 0.20 assign Timber plantation
ELSE IF tree-crop proportion > 0.20 assign Tree cropland
ELSE IF cropland proportion > 0.20 assign Cropland
ELSE IF protected proportion > 0.20 assign Protected land
ELSE assign Untransformed land
Example, if:

settlement proportion = 0.25;
cropland proportion = 0.30; and
both exceed 0.20.

The segment is assigned to Settlements, because settlements have higher priority than croplands.

Examples








Segment composition
Assigned class
Reason




15% settlement, 30% cropland, 55% untransformed
Croplands
Settlement does not exceed 20%, but cropland does


22% timber, 35% cropland, 43% untransformed
Timber plantations
Both exceed 20%, but timber has higher priority


10% cropland, 25% protected, 65% untransformed
Protected lands
Protected cover exceeds 20% and no higher-priority class does


10% settlement, 10% crop, 15% protected, 65% untransformed
Untransformed lands
No other class exceeds 20%


25% settlement inside a protected area
Settlements
Transformed land is assigned before protected land



Note, a higher-priority transformed land use can override the protected assignment.
The allocation logic is implemented in reverse order in GEE because later where() statements overwrite earlier assignments. In other words, “where” the condition is true, replace the current value with the specified class.
var assignedLandUse = ee.Image(BII_UNTRANSFORMED)

  .where(
    propProtected.gt(0.20),
    BII_PROTECTED
  )

  .where(
    propCropland.gt(0.20),
    BII_CROPLAND
  )

  .where(
    propTreeCrop.gt(0.20),
    BII_TREE_CROP
  )

  .where(
    propTimber.gt(0.20),
    BII_TIMBER
  )

  .where(
    propSettlement.gt(0.20),
    BII_SETTLEMENT
  )

  .rename('bii_land_use');

title: Broad land use allocation
Broad land use allocation
text:
Output
The final spatial product is a two-band raster:
bii_land_use
bii_land_use_intensity

Band 1: bii_land_use
An integer value from 1 to 6 representing the dominant BII land use class assigned to each segment.


Band 2: bii_land_use_intensity
A continuous value from 0 to 1 representing segment-level land use intensity. For non-natural classes, this combines the within-class intensity of the assigned land use with the proportion of the terrestrial segment covered by all non-natural land uses. See “land use intensity” for more detail.
The two bands must be interpreted together. The intensity value is conditional on the broad land use assigned to the segment, and the intensity of Untransformed lands will be refined separately using ecological pressure and condition information.
